summary: Describes an architecture for delay-tolerant and disruption-tolerant networks, evolved from the original design for the Interplanetary Internet, where links are long and often interrupted. This memo is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo describes an architecture for networks where links may be delayed, interrupted, or unavailable for long periods. A bundle layer stores messages and forwards them when communication becomes possible.

questions: what is custody transfer in dtn
how does dtn differ from tcp ip
how does a dtn node forward bundles
subtitle: A message-oriented overlay for networks with long delays, intermittent links, or extended disconnections.

tldr.problem: Internet protocols often assume a continuous end-to-end path and timely feedback, assumptions that fail in networks with long delays, frequent partitions, or intermittent links.
tldr.mechanism: A bundle layer stores variable-length messages in persistent storage and forwards them when communication contacts become available, with optional priorities, reports, custody transfer, and security.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4838 describes an architecture developed by the IRTF DTN research group. It is Informational and not a candidate for an Internet Standard.

today: RFC 4838 is an Informational RFC published in April 2007 and is a product of the Internet Research Task Force. It is not a candidate for an Internet Standard; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Delay-Tolerant Networking Is Needed
sections.content:
Conventional Internet protocols assume an end-to-end path remains available during a session, that timely feedback makes retransmission effective, and that end-to-end loss is relatively small. They also assume that all routers and end stations support TCP/IP.

The DTN architecture relaxes these assumptions. It targets deep-space communication as well as sensor networks with scheduled links, terrestrial wireless networks without ordinary end-to-end connectivity, satellite networks, and underwater acoustic networks. Its design uses variable-length messages, flexible names, storage within the network, coarse service classes, useful-lifetime information, and security controls.
sections.plainLanguage: Some networks cannot keep a path open while two applications exchange data. DTN is designed for those networks, where a message may need to wait before it can move again.

sections.title: The Bundle Layer, Nodes, and Endpoints
sections.content:
Applications send messages called Application Data Units (ADUs). The bundle layer, an overlay above underlying transport layers and below applications, turns them into bundles that DTN nodes forward. Bundles contain blocks for application data and delivery information, and can be fragmented and reassembled in the network.

A DTN endpoint is a set of nodes; a bundle is delivered when the endpoint's minimum reception group receives it. An Endpoint Identifier (EID) names an endpoint using URI syntax. The EID may be interpreted at the source, during transit, or at the destination, a method called late binding. Unlike ordinary IP store-and-forward, DTN nodes may keep bundles in persistent storage for extended periods and preserve them across restarts.
sections.plainLanguage: An application hands a message to the bundle layer, which packages it for forwarding between DTN nodes. Each node can store the bundle until it has a usable next connection.

sections.title: Contacts, Routing, and Fragmentation
sections.content:
The architecture models a DTN as a graph whose connections can vary over time and may work in only one direction. A period when a connection has positive capacity is called a contact. The memo names persistent, on-demand, scheduled, opportunistic, and predicted contacts. Knowing future contact times and capacities can help routing, while uncertain contacts make routing more difficult.

Fragmentation can help fit data into available contact capacity. Proactive fragmentation divides data into smaller bundles before transmission; the final destination reassembles them. Reactive fragmentation happens after a transfer is interrupted, allowing the remaining portion to be sent later. Reactive fragmentation is optional because it needs support from underlying protocols and can complicate signatures and authentication. Destination reassembly is required.
sections.plainLanguage: A contact is a time when a network connection can carry data. DTN can plan around known contacts or split a large bundle so that portions fit available opportunities.

sections.title: Priority, Reports, and Custody Transfer
sections.content:
Bundles may have relative priority classes: bulk, normal, and expedited. These priorities order bundles from the same source; policy determines whether priority is also compared across sources. Applications can request delivery options, including custody transfer, delivery reports, application acknowledgements, and diagnostic reports for reception, forwarding, custody acceptance, or deletion.

With custody transfer, a node accepts responsibility for reliable delivery and may pass that responsibility to another custodian. Custodians signal whether a transfer succeeded, and the bundle layer provides coarse timeouts and retransmission when requested. Custody transfer is advisory: not every node must accept custody. Without it, delivery relies on the underlying protocols. Administrative status reports go to a report-to EID, while custody signals go to the current custodian.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications can mark bundles as higher priority or ask for delivery reports. They can also ask a node to accept responsibility for forwarding, but a node may decline custody.

sections.title: Time, Resources, and Stored State
sections.content:
DTN nodes need time synchronization for bundle identification, scheduled or predicted routing, expiration, and application-registration expiration. A bundle includes a creation timestamp and a useful lifetime; it may be discarded after its lifetime ends. Its source EID, timestamp, and fragment offset and length together identify it.

Storage is a resource that must be managed. The memo says congestion and flow control at the bundle layer remain unresolved research topics, especially when storage is scarce and bundles may be held for long periods. Nodes may discard expired bundles, stop accepting custody, or discard non-custody bundles as necessary, but should avoid discarding bundles for which they accepted custody except as a last resort. Nodes also maintain application registrations, custody state, routing and forwarding information, security material, and policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Bundles have timestamps and lifetimes, and nodes keep state while they store and forward them. The memo leaves important questions about congestion and storage management for further research.

sections.title: Security, Applications, and Convergence Layers
sections.content:
DTN security is optional, but the memo says authentication and access control are needed in many environments where resources are scarce. Its goals include rejecting unauthorized traffic early, preventing unauthorized control of infrastructure, limiting traffic to authorized rates and service classes, detecting damaged or modified bundles, and identifying compromised entities. It describes hop-by-hop and end-to-end authentication and integrity; detailed security mechanisms are defined elsewhere.

Convergence layers adapt the bundle layer to each underlying protocol and provide a consistent interface. A TCP/IP convergence layer may only need to add message boundaries, while a less reliable protocol may require additional reliability, fragmentation, and flow control. Applications should minimize round trips, include enough information in each ADU to make it independent work, and preserve state across restarts while transactions remain pending. The memo gives a bundled file request as an example that may complete in one round trip, compared with up to eight for an FTP put.
sections.plainLanguage: Each underlying network needs an adapter, and security checks help protect scarce storage and links. Applications should send complete requests and preserve their state because a reply may arrive long after the program stops.
